title: Fermi estimates
objectives: Estimate a quantity by breaking it into parts you can guess.

screens.title: Water in a pool
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: how many litres of water are in an Olympic pool? Take it as 50 m long, 25 m wide and 2 m deep. One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres.

state.caption: Seen from above. Depth 2 m all over.

screens.question: Fill in the volume and the litres.

hints.text: Volume is length times width times depth.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the three dimensions, then convert to litres.

byKey.r4c1: Each cubic metre is 1,000 litres: $2{,}500 \times 1{,}000 = 2{,}500{,}000$. If you wrote 250,000, you multiplied by 100.

explain.text: Three factors multiply to 2,500 m³, and each cubic metre is 1,000 litres. So the pool holds 2,500,000 litres, about $2.5 \times 10^6$. Here every factor was given, so the answer is exact.

screens.title: Three guesses
screens.prose: Harder: how many trades does a market-making desk do in a day? Nobody gives you the factors now. Guess them: instruments quoted, fills per instrument per hour, and hours traded. Try each slider.
screens.question: Double any one factor. What happens to the total?

options.text: It doubles, whichever factor you double.
Doubling the largest factor moves it most.
options.why: You judged by the size of the factor. On the log axis every doubling moves the dot the same step.

options.text: It grows by the size of the factor you change.
options.why: You added instead of multiplying. Each factor scales the whole product.
The hours look small, but doubling 8 to 16 doubles the total too.

hints.text: Move one slider up one stop and read the caption.
Every doubling doubles the product: the dot moves the same distance each time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the totals before and after one step of any slider.

explain.text: A product scales with each factor, so doubling any one doubles the total. On a log axis that is the same step every time. A small factor is as important as a big one.

screens.title: A Fermi estimate
screens.prose: Breaking a quantity into factors you can guess is a **Fermi estimate**. Zhou’s green book and Crack’s *Heard on the Street* are full of them. Take the central guesses: 500 instruments, 20 fills each an hour, 8 hours.
screens.question: How many trades is that?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply instruments, fills an hour and hours.

byKey.no-hours: That is one hour of trading. Multiply by the 8 hours.
byKey.added: You added the factors. A Fermi estimate multiplies them.

explain.text: $500 \times 20 = 10{,}000$ fills an hour, and 8 hours make 80,000. Each factor is a guess, so the total is only as good as they are. Next we ask how good that is.

screens.title: Powers of ten
screens.prose: Interviewers want the order of magnitude first. Round each factor to one significant figure and count powers of ten: $5 \times 10^2$, $2 \times 10^1$ and $8$. This is the trick from Mental Maths Under Pressure, lesson 7.

state.caption: On a log axis, powers of ten are equally spaced

screens.question: Which power of ten is the total closest to?

options.why: You dropped two powers of ten. Count them: $10^2 \times 10^1$ is $10^3$, and $5 \times 2 \times 8 = 80$ adds nearly two more.
You counted the powers but forgot the leading digits. $5 \times 2 \times 8 = 80$, nearly another $10^2$.
You added a power of ten. 80,000 is just under $10^5$.

hints.text: Multiply the leading digits and add the powers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the leading digits, then add the powers of ten.

explain.text: The digits give $5 \times 2 \times 8 = 80$ and the powers give $10^3$. So the total is $8 \times 10^4$, closest to $10^5$ on a log scale. Say the magnitude before the digits.

screens.title: How good is the guess?
screens.prose: Each guess could be half or double. Say 250 to 1,000 instruments, 10 to 40 fills an hour, and 4 to 16 hours.
screens.question: Fill in the lowest and highest totals.

hints.text: Multiply the low column, then the high column.
Low 10,000; high 640,000. Each is a factor of 8 from 80,000.

feedback.correct: 10,000 to 640,000: a factor of 8 each way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply all three lows, and all three highs.

byKey.r3c1: $250 \times 10 \times 4 = 10{,}000$. If you wrote 40,000, you halved only one factor.
byKey.r3c3: $1{,}000 \times 40 \times 16 = 640{,}000$. If you wrote 160,000, you doubled only one factor.

explain.text: Three factors each off by 2 compound to a factor of $2^3 = 8$. So the range is 10,000 to 640,000 around 80,000. On a log axis each factor adds the same step of doubt.

screens.title: False precision
screens.prose: Another candidate guesses 487 instruments, 23 fills an hour and 8.5 hours. They multiply and announce: "95,209 trades a day."

state.caption: Three guesses, each good to a factor of 2

screens.question: How should the answer be given?

options.text: "About 100,000, good to a factor of 8 either way."

options.why: You kept five figures from three guesses. The digits after the first carry no information.
You kept even the half trade. Guessed factors cannot support that, and trades come whole.
You threw away the estimate. A factor of 8 each way is honest; ten million times is not.

hints.text: How many of the digits come from real knowledge?
Each factor is good to a factor of 2.
Round to one significant figure and say the uncertainty: about $10^5$, within a factor of 8.

feedback.correct: About $10^5$, with the factor of 8 stated.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the precision of the answer to the precision of the guesses.

byKey.precise: You kept five figures from three guesses. That is false precision.
byKey.exact: You kept even the half trade. That is false precision.

explain.text: Three guesses good to a factor of 2 make a total good to a factor of 8. So "about 100,000" is honest and "95,209" only looks precise. Say the magnitude and the uncertainty.

screens.title: A closed market
screens.prose: The interviewer adds a twist: estimate the desk’s trades on Christmas Day. The exchange is shut, so the desk trades for 0 hours.
screens.question: What is your estimate now?

widget.accept: 0: a product with a zero factor is zero.
widget.label: Trades

hints.text: What does multiplying by zero do?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One factor is zero.

byKey.usual: That is a normal day. The hours factor is now 0.
byKey.skip: You left the zero factor out. It sets the whole product to zero.

explain.text: One zero factor makes the whole product zero, however large the others are. Always ask whether a factor can vanish: a holiday, a halted share, a closed venue. Then say the answer is zero, with zero width.

screens.title: Errors in logs
screens.prose: Logs turn a product into a sum. $$\ln Q = \ln f_1 + \ln f_2 + \ln f_3.$$ If factor $i$ is good to a factor $r_i$, the total is good to about $r_1 r_2 r_3$. Relative errors add, in logs.
screens.question: Four factors, each good to a factor of 2. The total is good to a factor of what?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the four factors of 2.

byKey.three: That is three factors. The question has four.
byKey.no-compound: You assumed the errors do not compound. In the worst case they all line up.
byKey.added: You counted the factors of 2 instead of multiplying them.

explain.text: In logs each factor adds $\ln 2$, so four of them add $4 \ln 2 = \ln 16$. Undo the log: a factor of 16. That is the worst case; errors that cancel give less.

screens.title: Why errors multiply
screens.prose: Show why a product of guesses is good to the product of their factors. Each $f_i$ lies between $c_i / r_i$ and $c_i r_i$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order, and leave out the false step.

lines.text: $Q = f_1 f_2 f_3$, the estimate is a product
$\ln Q = \ln f_1 + \ln f_2 + \ln f_3$, the log of a product is a sum
each $\ln f_i$ is within $\ln r_i$ of $\ln c_i$, since $c_i / r_i \le f_i \le c_i r_i$
$\ln Q$ is within $\ln r_1 + \ln r_2 + \ln r_3 = \ln(r_1 r_2 r_3)$ of $\ln(c_1 c_2 c_3)$, adding the bounds
$Q$ is within a factor $r_1 r_2 r_3$ of $c_1 c_2 c_3$, undoing the log
$Q$ is within $r_1 + r_2 + r_3$ of $c_1 c_2 c_3$, adding the error factors
lines.why: Error factors multiply. They add only after taking logs.

hints.text: Start from the product, then take logs.
In logs, each factor’s doubt is a plus or minus $\ln r_i$.
Product, log, each bound, add the bounds, undo the log.

feedback.correct: Logs turn multiplied errors into added ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take logs before adding anything.

byKey.bad: Error factors multiply. They add only after taking logs.
byKey.left-out: Every true line belongs in the derivation. Only the line adding the error factors is false.

explain.text: Taking logs turns the product into a sum, so the bounds add. Undoing the log turns the added bounds into a multiplied factor. For three factors of 2 that is $2^3 = 8$.

screens.title: Fermi in code
screens.prose: Keep each guess as a triple: low, central, high. The product of the lows is the lowest total, and so on. `math.prod` multiplies a list.
screens.question: Complete `fermi_product(factors)`.

widget.starter:
from math import prod


def fermi_product(factors):
    """factors: a list of (low, central, high) guesses.
    Return (low, central, high) of their product."""
    ...
widget.solution:
from math import prod


def fermi_product(factors):
    """factors: a list of (low, central, high) guesses.
    Return (low, central, high) of their product."""
    low = prod(f[0] for f in factors)
    central = prod(f[1] for f in factors)
    high = prod(f[2] for f in factors)
    return (low, central, high)
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each result must equal the exact products of the lows, the centres and the highs.

hints.text: `prod(f[0] for f in factors)` multiplies the lows.
Return `(prod of lows, prod of centres, prod of highs)`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Multiply each column of guesses on its own.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
The lows multiply to the lowest total and the highs to the highest. Integers and fractions stay exact, and a zero factor gives zero everywhere. The desk example gives 10,000, 80,000 and 640,000.

```python
return (prod(f[0] for f in factors), prod(f[1] for f in factors), prod(f[2] for f in factors))
```

screens.title: The interviewer trades
screens.prose: The interviewer lists a contract paying £1 for every 1,000 trades the desk does today. Your fair value is 80. You offer to sell at 90, and the interviewer buys 3. Mark the ledger at your fair value.
screens.question: What is your P&L at your fair value, in pounds?

widget.accept: £30: 3 contracts sold £10 above your fair value.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

hints.text: How far above your fair value did you sell?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A seller makes the price minus the value, on each contract.

byKey.sign: You sold above your value, so on your numbers you gain.
byKey.one: That is one contract. The interviewer bought 3.
byKey.cash: That is the cash received. Subtract what the 3 contracts are worth to you, £240.

explain.text: On your numbers you made £30. But someone keen to buy 3 at 90 may think the count is higher than 90. Lesson 5 turns that into a two-sided price, and lesson 7 moves it after a trade.

screens.title: How much will trade?
screens.prose: Before quoting a contract at a charity trading game, size the market. There are 40 traders. Each trades about 5 times in the 30-minute game, 2 contracts a time.
screens.question: How many contracts might trade in the game?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply traders, trades each and contracts a trade.

byKey.no-size: That counts trades, not contracts. Each trade is 2 contracts.
byKey.added: You added the factors. Multiply them.

explain.text: About 400 contracts should trade, good to a factor of a few. So quote a size of a few contracts, not 100: one fill must not swamp the game. The Fermi number sets how large to quote, and the next lessons set how wide.

ideas: A Fermi estimate multiplies factors you can guess; say the power of ten first.
In logs the doubts add: three factors each good to 2 make a total good to $2^3 = 8$.
Report one significant figure with its uncertainty, and check for a factor that can be zero.

formula.name: Error of a product
formula.note: The worst case, when every error lines up.

summary.trap: False precision: five figures from three guesses, or one wild factor hidden in a confident total.

quiz.prose: A market is open 8.5 hours a day for 252 trading days a year.
quiz.question: How many trading minutes is that in a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply days, hours and minutes.

byKey.hours: That is the hours. Multiply by 60 for minutes.
byKey.calendar: That uses 365 days. The market opens on 252.

explain.text: $252 \times 8.5 = 2{,}142$ hours, and $2{,}142 \times 60 = 128{,}520$ minutes. That is about $1 \times 10^5$.

quiz.prose: A Fermi estimate has four factors. Two are good to a factor of 2, one to a factor of 3, and one is exact.
quiz.question: The total is good to a factor of what?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the error factors; an exact factor contributes 1.

byKey.added: You added the error factors. They multiply.
byKey.worst: You kept only the worst factor. The others compound with it.

explain.text: Error factors multiply: $2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 1 = 12$. The exact factor adds no doubt. In logs, $\ln 2 + \ln 2 + \ln 3 = \ln 12$.

options.why: You kept ten figures from guessed factors. That is false precision.

options.text: Somewhere between a million and a trillion.
options.why: You threw the estimate away. One significant figure with a factor of doubt is enough.
